sentences.text: The known specimen of Scansoriopteryx heilmanni represents the remains of a hatchling maniraptoran dinosaur that was roughly the size of a sparrow.
This animal possessed an unusual, elongated third finger where long wing feathers appear to attach rather than the middle digit.
Its pubis bone pointed forward, representing a primitive trait among theropods.
Short legs featured small pebbly scales and possible impressions of long feathers on the upper foot.
An unusually large first toe may have been reversed to allow grasping.
An elongated third finger likely supported a membranous wing structure.
Fossils preserve wispy, down-like feathers forming V-shaped patterns similar to modern down feathers.
Unlike modern bird hatchlings, this creature had forelimbs longer than its hind limbs.
The genus Scansoriopteryx was described and named by Czerkas and Yuan in 2002.
It is known from a single juvenile fossil specimen discovered in Liaoning, China, which Czerkas and Yuan initially reported likely came from the Yixian Formation.
Czerkas and Yuan initially reported that the specimen likely came from the Yixian Formation.
Researchers interpreted the hallux as reversed, a condition common in modern tree-dwelling birds.
Scientists suggest the animal may have used its tail as a prop, similar to modern woodpeckers.
Czerkas and Yuan speculated that adults may have had wing feathers for leaping or gliding, but ruled out powered flight.
Czerkas and Yuan argued that Scansoriopteryx possessed primitive and birdlike characters that supported an unorthodox interpretation of dinosaur evolution.
Scansoriopteryx is classified as a member of the clade Avialae and is considered a close relative of true birds.
The genus Scansoriopteryx gave its name to the family Scansoriopterygidae.
Most researchers consider the genus Scansoriopteryx to be a synonym of Epidendrosaurus.
The fossil range of Scansoriopteryx spans from the Callovian to the Oxfordian stages, though other sources suggest it lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages.
The holotype skeleton of Epidendrosaurus was recovered from the Daohugou fossil beds in northeastern China.
The age of the Daohugou beds has been estimated anywhere from 169 million years ago in the Middle Jurassic to 122 million years ago in the Early Cretaceous.
The exact age of the Daohugou formation is debated because it affects understanding of Epidendrosaurus relationships and the origin of birds.
There is a scientific debate regarding whether Scansoriopteryx is a senior synonym or a junior synonym of the genus Epidendrosaurus.
The hypothesis that Scansoriopteryx evolved from non-dinosaurian archosaurs rather than being a dinosaur has been overwhelmingly rejected by paleontologists.
